Question: Have you ever lost any respect for someone instantly?
Answer: Yes! This question reflexly reminds me of a scene at the coffee-counter of a Bengaluru restaurant. It might have easily been a year ago! Well, I was at this restaurant opposite to our hospital at Rajajinagar, waiting for my cup of coffee. I’d been in the locality for a while and the person handling the coffee counter is a quiet, unassuming and pleasant guy, as I know him. As I was waiting, I couldn’t help but hear the conversation the lady customer before me in the queue was having with the coffee guy. The conversation was in Kannada. I have included the English translation within parentheses. Lady: Enuuu, ninne kaaNle illa…! elli hogidri? (Where had you gone yesterday? you were not seen around!) Coffee guy: Huun, ninne bandirlilla. Maganige laptop kodsbekithu. (Yes, I had not come yesterday. I had to buy my son a laptop.) Lady: First hand a, second hand a?! (A new one or second-hand one?!) Coffee guy (quite abashed): First hand e ne (A new one indeed) That moment, my respect for that lady came crashing down! I’d never lost respect for a stranger that quickly ever before. Whilst it might be deemed a very normal conversation by many, personally I would never ever ask such a weird question! I might ask for the price, make, or if it was touchscreen, but never if it was second-hand! I kept wondering what kind of thought process a person should possess to make him/ her think that the child of a restaurant worker should get only ‘second-hand’ things in life! The fact that, that was the first question which popped in her mind only makes it worse. Just not done!

Name: Dr. Balakrishnan Ramanan
Question: Which is your favourite Tamil dialect and why?
Answer: I was born in a Tamil Iyer family, but was brought up speaking as neutral a Tamil dialect as possible! By convention, I don’t speak the Brahmin Tamil dialect or fake it to display my caste to the listener(s). As a student, I loved Tamil literature in school. Tamil used to be my most favourite subject throughout. I would read all the poems and most lessons the very day I receive the books. I’ve always written my own essays in exams. From grade 10 and later, I also started writing my own poems. So much was my love for the standard Tamil. English was a close second. I was always interested in arts and literature. (And landed up in Medicine years later :D).  I live in Pondicherry, where the Tamil dialect can be considered very close to that in Chennai. But the aforesaid love for the Tamil language and my upbringing meant that I wouldn’t like or acquire the colloquial dialect as well. Because of my extended family, media and friends from all over Tamil Nadu, I’ve had the privilege to hear and familiarise myself with most, if not all, dialects of Tamil. I was quite familiar with the Kongu Tamil, Madurai Tamil, Sri Lankan Tamil and the ‘Madras baashai’! Coming to the question now, if I’d have to choose a single Tamil dialect as ‘favourite’, it would be the Tirunelveli dialect! I had not heard much of it, though I knew this dialect existed. It is quite a unique dialect, clearly distinct from the Madurai dialect (these two dialects are often misconstrued to be one and the same). I fell in love with this beautiful dialect, after having watched the movie ‘Papanasam’ (2015) starring Kamal Haasan. He is of course, a legendary actor known to perform diverse roles and ace multiple languages in multiple dialects (including the Uttara Karnataka dialect of Kannada and Telangana dialect of Telugu). Question: Why doesn't the Karnataka government rename Rajajinagar and Kamaraj Road to Kannada names?
Answer: For the simple reason that both were national leaders/ political figures, and not merely politicians limited to Tamil Nadu. C Rajagopalachari aka Rajaji was the first and last Governor General of independent India. He was also the Union Minister for Home Affairs between 1950 and 1951.[1] K Kamaraj was the president of Indian National Congress (the only major political party at that time) between 1964 and 1967. Not just that, he is known as the ‘kingmaker’ of the then Indian politics for he was responsible for making Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi the Prime Ministers after the demise of Jawaharlal Nehru.[2] Both Rajaji and K Kamaraj, therefore, have a nationwide appeal and historical importance. Also, let’s not forget that both of them were active players in the Indian freedom struggle! With Bengaluru being the capital of the Indian state of Karnataka, at least I don’t see a compelling reason to rename the said area and the said road! Bro, but what about the kannadathana of the city? Well, The above list is only a handful, based on my knowledge of the areas in and around my home in Bengaluru. There are hundreds of other areas/ roads/ places in the city named after Kannadigas, or depicting Kannada culture. For instance, Sampige Road at Malleshwara is named in Kannada after the flower that’s widely available and sold in the area. Having said all that, a couple of Tamils’ names doesn’t have to warrant a riot! (A frame from Rajajinagar; from my phone’s gallery)
